column2: As water poured from another source is added to that same water in a pond, so the aged one gains increase, as water in water.
So whatever deeds here are joined with intellect, lord of the earth, are not lowered, even if among the most meritorious.
The king should conquer the armed and the haughty, and rightly protect the subjects; he should kindle fire with many sacrifices, and at the end or the middle he should resort to the forest.
A self-controlled man, devoted to dharma, learned, should see beings as himself; he should honour the greater according to his power, by truth and character, lord of men, in happiness.
One who has been cast off with respect, without affection, should be avoided, even a brother of the same womb, how much more another common person.
Giving and receiving between the distinguished and the more distinguished are equal; the gift of one who gives to a twice-born is the more meritorious.
Wealth gained justly by the classes and increased justly should be guarded with effort for the sake of dharma: so it is settled.
One who seeks dharma should not gain wealth by cruel deed; he should do all tasks as able and should not think of prosperity.
Water, cold or warmed by fire, given to a guest according to ability, and food to the hungry, bring fruit.
Rantideva, the great soul, gained the success desired in the worlds; he honoured sages with fruit, leaves and roots.
With those same fruit and leaves he satisfied the Mathara; from it Shaibya, lord of the earth, gained the highest place.
Mortal beings are born in debt to gods, guests, servants, ancestors and the self; therefore one should go to freedom from debt.
Ushanas, by propitiating the god of gods, reached the state of Shukra; having praised the goddess he rejoices in the sky, covered with energy.
Asita and Devala, Narada and Parvata, Kakshivan, Jamadagnya, Rama, Tandya and Anshuman,
Vasishtha, Jamadagni, Vishvamitra and Atri, Bharadvaja, Harishmashru, Kundadhara and Shrutashrava:
these great sages, collected, praising Vishnu with Rik verses, gained success by austerity through the grace of the wise one.
The unworthy, praising him alone, became worthy; but one should not seek increase here by doing a despised deed.
Wealth that is by dharma is real; shame on that which is by adharma; one should not give up eternal dharma in the world from desire for wealth.
The righteous-souled one who has set up the fires is the best doer of merit; for all the Vedas, king of kings, stand in the three fires.
And that brahmana who has set up the fires, whose rites do not lapse, is good; for not having set up the fires is the good; fire-offering is not inaction.
Fire, the self, the mother, the father who begot, and the teacher: tiger among men, these are to be served properly.

The man who, giving up pride, serves the aged, learned, though a eunuch he sees out of affection, not lacking skill, joined with dharma, not self-controlled: he is honoured in this world by the good, noble.
If a shudra has no livelihood from his father and grandfather's firm one, he should not seek livelihood elsewhere but should engage in service.
Association with the good, who see dharma, is beautiful, always and in every state, not with the bad: so I hold.
As a thing shines by nearness to the mountain of dawn, so even one of low class shines by nearness to the good.
By whatever colour a white garment is dyed, it takes that form; know this to be so for me.
Therefore be attached to virtues and never to faults; the life of mortals here is unsteady and moving.
The wise, whether in happiness or in sorrow, who gathers only good things sees good things here.
An action apart from dharma, even if of great fruit, the wise should not do; it is not said to be beneficial.
The king who, having taken thousands of cows, gives them without protecting is only a thief who shares the fruit of a word.
By shudras not crooked, not deceitful, not angry, who prepare oblations and offerings, the cleansing should be done, and so dharma is not lost.
When dharma is not lost, the subjects are happy; and by their happiness, king, the gods in heaven rejoice.
Therefore the king who protects is honoured with dharma; so too the brahmana who studies, the vaishya intent on earning,
and the shudra who serves constantly with controlled senses. Otherwise, lord of men, one falls from his own dharma.
Even small coins, assigned from distress of breath, are of great fruit if justly earned and given; how much more others by thousands.
He who gives to the twice-born with honour always enjoys the vigorous fruit, such as it is, king.
What is given after going to the person, with satisfaction, they call blessed and praised; what is given on request, the wise call middling.
What is given with contempt and also without faith, truth-speaking sages call the lowest gift.
Sinking in transgression of many kinds, a man should always make effort so as to be freed from doubt.
The brahmana shines by self-control, the kshatriya by victory, the vaishya by wealth, and the shudra ever shines by skill.
Of the three classes the shudra is always called the server; one who follows kshatriya dharma and vaishya dharma does not fall; but when a twice-born does shudra work, then he falls.
Trade, herding and living by crafts are enjoined even for a shudra when livelihood is not found.
Stage-acting and living by such arts, living by liquor and meat, and selling iron and leather:
a blamed work in the world should not be done by one who has not done it before; for one who has done it and gives it up, there is great dharma, so scripture says.
A man who commits sin in the world with a mind soaked in intoxication has accomplishment that is not called acceptable.
It is heard in the Purana that the subjects were ruled by the rod of "Shame!"; self-controlled, chief in dharma, following the dharma of justice.
Dharma alone is always praised here for men, king; men on earth, grown in dharma, serve only virtues.
That dharma the asuras could not bear, dear, lord of men; as they grew, in order, the subjects entered them there.
Then, overcome by anger, their conduct that had modesty and shame lost even modesty, king, and delusion was born.
Then, covered with delusion, they did not see as before, and lived as they pleased, crushing each other.
Reaching them, that rod of "Shame!" was no longer the cause; then they turned to the gods and despised the brahmanas.
At this very time the gods went for refuge to the best god Shiva, the hero of many forms, lord of hosts.
By him, in the sky, with one arrow, strengthened by the gods' energy, the three cities were felled to the ground.
Their lord was dreadful, of dreadful valour, a terror to the gods; he was slain by the trident-bearer.
When he was slain, men regained their own state, and the Vedas and shastras went on as before.
Then they anointed Vasava in heaven with the kingdom of the gods, and the seven sages appointed him to hold the rod over men.
Above the seven sages was the king named Viprithu; kings and kshatriyas were in the circles, each separately.
In the great families, those born and those earlier, the asuric feeling does not leave their hearts.
Therefore, by that same feeling with its attachment, mighty kings practised only asuric deeds.
They established themselves in those very ones and set them up, and the most childish men follow them even today.
Therefore I say to you, king: having reflected from the shastras, one should do a work that brings perfection, and give up work of a violent nature.
The wise should not accumulate wealth through confusion; giving up justice for the sake of dharma and wealth is not called good.
So you, such a one, self-controlled, a kshatriya dear to kinsmen, protect subjects, servants and sons by your own dharma.
Meeting of the wished and unwished, enmity and friendship: so many thousands of births turn about.
Therefore be attached to virtues and never to faults; the ill-minded without virtues is called an enemy of himself.
Dharma and adharma operate among men, great king, not so among other beings, here without humans.
The man of dharmic character, learned, whether active or inactive, should ever go about in the world as the self of beings, harming no beings.
When his mind is rid of the written mark, and there is no falsehood in it, then he gains the good."
[Parashara said:] "For the most part the sense of mine arises in a householder, from attachment, best of men, with tamasic and rajasic states.
Houses, cows, fields, wealth, wives, sons and servants come to a man here.
For him so engaged, ever looking at this, attachment and aversion grow, as he does not see impermanence.
To a man overcome by attachment and aversion and following wealth, lord of men, a delight born of delusion comes.
Having achieved his end by enjoyment, intent on delight, he sees no gain other than the pleasure of the village, from delight.
Then, with a self overcome by greed, he increases people through attachment, and for his nourishment wishes to do the people's wealth here.
Though knowing what should not be done, a man does it for wealth, with a self full of child-like affection, and then repents at its loss.
Then, endowed with pride, guarding his own defeat, he does what makes him an enjoyer, and for that perishes.
From disgust comes knowledge of the self; from knowledge, the vision of scripture; from vision of the meaning of scripture, king, he sees austerity alone.
A man of reflection is hard to find, lord of men, who, when pleasure is spent, resolves to practise austerity.
Austerity is for all, dear, even for the low; for the self-controlled, restrained, it shows the path to heaven.
Prajapati, the lord, created the subjects formerly through austerity; somewhere devoted to vows, taking up vows, king.
Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Agni, Ashvins, Maruts, Vishvedevas, Sadhyas, ancestors and hosts of Maruts,
yakshas, rakshasas, gandharvas, perfected ones and other dwellers in heaven, and others who live in heaven, were perfected by austerity, dear.
The brahmanas created in the beginning by Brahma formerly through austerity roam, making the earth and heaven flourish.
Kings in the world of mortals and other householders seen in great families: all that is the fruit of austerity.
Silk garments, lovely ornaments, vehicles, seats and carriages: all that is the fruit of austerity.
Thousands of beautiful women agreeable to the mind, dwelling on palace roofs: all that is the fruit of austerity.
The best beds and varied foods, all wished for, come to those who have done the work.
Nothing is unattainable by austerity in these three worlds, scourge of foes; giving up enjoyment is the fruit for those who have not done the work.
Happy or unhappy, a man should give up greed, considering the shastra with mind and intellect, best of kings.
Discontent leads only to unhappiness; from greed comes confusion of the senses; then his wisdom is lost, like learning without practice.
When wisdom is lost he does not see justice; therefore, when pleasure is spent, a man should practise fierce austerity.
What is wished they call happiness; what is hated, sorrow here; see the fruit of austerity done and not done, such as it is.
They always see good things and enjoy objects, and by doing stainless austerity they become radiant.
The disagreeable and insults, sorrow of many kinds: the seeker of fruit who gives up that path gains the objects.
Doubt about dharma, austerity and giving arises in him, and having done sin he goes to hell.
The man whose eye is scripture, and who in happiness or in sorrow, best of men, does not stray from his own conduct, is the man.
Delight in the touch of contact is held to last only the flight of an arrow, in taste, sight, smell and hearing, lord of the people.
Then from its loss keen pain arises again; by which the wise praise liberation as the supreme happiness.
Then he acts for the fruit, and the virtues become superior; by the conduct of dharma he is never deprived of desire and wealth.
Objects that come without effort should always be enjoyed by householders, and those to be reached by effort are one's own dharma: so I hold.
For the proud, well-born, ever having the eye of scripture, deprived of acts of dharma, with self restrained by incapacity,
when the work being done goes to ruin for men, there is no work for them in the world except austerity.
With his whole self the householder should make a settled decision in action; he should go through his own dharma with skill for the offerings to gods and ancestors, king.
As all rivers and streams go to the ocean that stands, so all in the stages go to the householder who stands."
[Janaka said:] "The scripture says, 'what is born as offspring is the same one'; how then, born of a brahmana, is a distinction taken up?"
[Parashara said:] "So it is, great king; who begets is that very one; but by the lowering of austerity he is counted by birth.
From good field and good seed the origin is holy; from deficiency in either, a lower one is born.
From the mouth, the arms, the thighs and the feet they were born, as Prajapati created the worlds: so the knowers of dharma know.
From the mouth, dear, the brahmanas; from the arms the kshatriyas; from the thighs the rich, king; from the feet the servants.
The origin is of four classes only, bull among men; others, beyond these, are remembered as born of mixture.
The kshatriya births, Ambashthas, Ugras and Vaidehakas, Shvapakas, Pulkasas, Stenas, Nishadas, Sutas and Magadhas,
Ayogas, Karanas, Vratyas and Chandalas, lord of men: these are born from the four classes among each other."
[Parashara said:] "King, this is to be accepted: from a lowly birth there arises a great-souled one among those whose selves are formed by austerity.
The sages, having begotten sons here and there on women of kings, made them sages again by their own austerity.
My grandfather before, and Rishyashringa, Kashyapa, Vatsa, Tandya, Kripa, Kakshivan, Kamatha and others,
Yavakrita, king, and Drona, best of speakers, Ayu, Matanga, Datta, Drupada and Matsya:
these, Vaideha, reached their nature by relying on austerity; they are the Vedic scholars established in self-control and austerity.
Four root gotras arose, lord of the earth: Angiras, Kashyapa, Vasishtha and Bhrigu.
Other gotras arose from action, lord of the earth; and the names by austerity too are the acceptance of the good."
[Janaka said:] "Tell me, blessed one, the special dharmas of the classes and the common dharmas also; for you are skilled in all."
[Parashara said:] "Receiving, officiating and teaching are the special dharma of brahmanas, king; protection is the fair one for the kshatriya.
Farming, herding and trade for vaishyas; service of the twice-born is the shudra's work, lord of men.
The special dharmas of the classes have been told; hear now in detail, dear, the common dharmas.
Non-cruelty, non-violence, heedfulness, sharing, shraddha rites, hospitality, truth and freedom from anger,
contentment with one's own wives, purity, constant freedom from envy, knowledge of the self and endurance are the common dharmas, king.
Brahmanas, kshatriyas and vaishyas are the three twice-born classes; they have authority in the dharmas here, best of two-footed beings.
The three classes, king, fall when standing in wrong action; they rise by resorting to the good in their own duties here.
It is not settled that a shudra falls, nor that he is not fit for the rites; he does not gain a dharma prompted by scripture, but no prohibition has been made for his dharma.
The twice-born, learned in scripture, cite the Vaideha as a shudra, great king; I see the god Vishnu, lord of the universe, the chief of the world.
Having followed the conduct of the good, the lowly who wish to rise up are not harmed, doing nourishing rites without mantra.
As other people take up good conduct, so they find happiness and rest here and hereafter."
[Janaka said:] "Great sage, what stains him, action or birth? Doubt has arisen in me; you should explain it."
[Parashara said:] "Without doubt, great king, both cause fault, action and birth; but learn the difference.
One who by birth and by action practises bad action; and one who is bad by birth but does not commit sin is a man.
A man chief by birth who does a blamed action: that action stains him; therefore action is not good.
[Janaka said:] "What actions are righteous in this world, best of the twice-born, which do not harm beings even when always done?"
[Parashara said:] "Hear from me, great king, what you ask me: the actions that are non-violent which always save a man.
Those who have renounced the fires, sitting, seeing, free of fever, having climbed the path of dharma leading to the highest good in due order,
humble, disciplined, ever self-controlled and of strict vow, go to the ageless state, free of all action.
All classes, having rightly done acts of dharma, king, and spoken true words, having given up dreadful adharma in the world of the living, go to heaven; there is no doubt in this."
[Parashara said:] "The father is the supreme deity of men; they say the father is better than the mother; they call gain of knowledge supreme; those whose senses are conquered obtain the highest.
In the field of battle, on a bed of arrows and fire, a king's son who meets death is burnt and goes to worlds hard for the immortals to reach, and enjoys heaven's fruit at will.
A king should not kill one who is weary, afraid, with weapon dropped, weeping, facing away, without retinue, undaunted, sick or begging, nor children and the aged.
A king in battle may overcome a kshatriya's son who is well supplied with retinue, ready and equal.
Here killing an equal or a superior is better, so it is settled; the killing of one lowly or timid is blamed for kings.
The killing of the sinful, of sinful conduct, and the lowly, lord of men, is called sin leading to hell: so it is settled.
No one saves, king, one who has come under the power of fate; and someone may be drawn away even when a remainder of life is left.
One should turn back from the actions done here by those with affection; one should not wish life from violent actions with long life.
The body is an aggregate of veins, sinew and bone, repulsive and crowded with impure things, a meeting of the elements, senses and qualities.
The learned thinkers on the self call the body ending in skin; again wasted, it comes to mortality.
Abandoned by the embodied one, motionless and without consciousness, it reaches the elements and sinks into the earth.
Joined with action by yoga, he is born here and there; this body, Vaideha, dies here and there; another nature is seen, and likewise the release of action.
The embodied one is never born of time alone, king; he turns about, as a great cloud in the sky.
He is born again, king, reaching a dwelling here; the self is beyond the mind, and the mind beyond the senses.
Among beings of two kinds, king, the moving are supreme; among the moving, the two-footed are held supreme; and among two-footed, the twice-born are remembered as supreme.
Among the twice-born, king of kings, those with wisdom are supreme; among the wise, those awake to the self; among the awakened, those without pride.
Death follows what is born: so it is settled for men; actions have an end, and beings follow the qualities.
When the sun has reached its highest point, he who meets death, in a star and at a moment that is holy, king, is a doer of merit.
Without engaging people in affliction, having crossed his bad deeds, having done his work by his own power, death here by an uncommon death...
Poison, hanging, burning, and slaying at the hands of robbers, by fanged beasts and animals, are called a common death.
Those of holy deeds are not joined with these, nor with those born of intention, nor with many such other common ones.
The breaths of those who do holy deeds leave upward, king; of those of middle merit through the middle; of those of bad deeds, below.
There is one enemy, no second enemy, for a man, king: ignorance; covered by it, joined, he does dreadful and very cruel deeds.
For awakening, what is joined with scripture and dharma and should be served by the aged, he is accomplished by effort, a king's son; churned by the arrow of wisdom, he goes.

Having studied the Vedas with austerity as a celibate, having performed the five sacrifices as able, a man who desires dharma should go to the forest, having gathered the good and established his lineage.
Even abandoned by enjoyments, one should not dishearten oneself; human birth, even among the Chandalas, is in every way hard to get, dear.
This is the first womb, having attained which, lord of the earth, the self can be saved by deeds of auspicious marks.
How shall we not be lost from this womb? so men practise dharma, seeing the authority of scripture.
The man who, having obtained the hardest-to-obtain human birth here, scorns dharma and is desire-natured is surely cheated.
He who sees with an eye led by affection, dear, beings like lamps, as long as the flame does not die,
by conciliation, giving and pleasant speech, equal in pleasure and pain, is honoured hereafter.
Giving, renunciation, a beautiful form, again the body bathed in the waters by austerity, Sarasvati, Naimisha and Pushkara and the other holy regions on earth:
for those whose breath falls in their houses, the carrying out is praised, the conveying to the cremation ground, and the burning by rule with purity.
Sacrifice, nourishing, worship, officiating, giving, the performance of meritorious acts, and whatever is praised as an ancestral rite, all he does for the self's sake as a man.
The dharmashastras, the Vedas and the six limbs are ordained for the good of the man of unwearied action, lord of men."
[Bhishma said:] "All this was told by the great-souled sage to the king of Videha long ago for his good, lord of men."
[Janaka said:] "What is the good, what the goal, brahmana? What done is not lost? Where gone does one not return? Tell me that, great sage."
[Parashara said:] "Non-attachment is the root of the good; knowledge, and the goal of knowledge, is supreme; austerity practised is not lost, as seed sown in a field is not lost.
When, having cut the snare of adharma, one delights in dharma, having given the gift made of fearlessness, then he gains success.
He who gives thousands of cows and hundreds of horses: fearlessness to all beings surpasses that gift.
The wise man, though living amid objects, does not live there; the fool lives with the wicked, even amid objects.
Adharma does not cling to the wise, as water to a lotus leaf; to the unwise greater sin clings, like lac to wood.
Adharma does not wait for a cause to release the doer; the doer reaches all of it in time; the self-trained, who see by the self's conviction, are not split.
The heedless who do not understand intellect, action and senses, with a self attached to good and bad, meet very great fear.
He gives up his wives, he does not strive for wealth, good horses and carriages, and the varied rites; when a man's mind is set on the third heaven, his intellect is split on objects.
The man whose mind is attached to objects, who never understands his own good, is dragged by the thought that follows all states, like a fish by a king's bait.
The world of mortals is an aggregate, depending on each other, like the pith of a plantain, and sinks like a boat in water.
There is no appointed time for dharma for a man, nor does death wait for a man; the action of dharma is always beautiful when the man is turned to the mouth of death.
As a blind man at home, by practice, goes his way, so with a mind joined, the wise man goes that goal.
Death is said to belong to birth, and birth rests on death; the unlearned, bound in the dharmas of liberation, wanders like a wheel.
As a lotus fibre quickly frees itself from mud that clings, so the self of a man here is freed by the mind; the mind leads the self and joins it.
Acting for another, he who thinks it his own affair, attached to objects of the senses, is deprived of his own affair.
The self of the wise and the other gains below, animal birth, and in heaven the highest goal, by its own deeds.
As liquid is put in a baked earthen vessel, so the body heated by austerity gains the object.
He who enjoys objects will not, without doubt, be an enjoyer; but he who gives up enjoyments, that self is fit to enjoy.
Covered by mist, intent on the organ and belly, like one blind from birth, with covered self, he does not know the road.
As a merchant gains wealth from the sea according to purpose, so in the ocean of mortality the course of a creature is by knowledge of action.
In a world made of days and nights, moving in the form of old age, death swallows beings, as a serpent the wind.
A creature born meets the deeds it has done; no one gets anything, pleasant or unpleasant, he has not done.
Whether lying, going, sitting, or engaged in objects, good and bad deeds ever follow a man."
Then the great-souled Agni said to those best of brahmanas, "For my own purpose I ask for Duryodhana's daughter."
How, brahmana, having sacrificed for the lord of the gods who is immortal, would you sacrifice without doubt for Marutta, who is joined with death?
Having said so, the righteous-souled aged king, bull of the Kurus, the wise one, took refuge with Gandhari, suddenly like one lifeless.
Then, entering the city of Dvaravati, Janardana said to his father: "Please guard all our women, awaiting Dhananjaya's coming. Rama waits for me at the forest's edge; I shall meet him today."
Where she is, the tall dark-skinned Draupadi, endowed with understanding and goodness, best of women, and where my beloved is.
Where Mandhata the royal sage is, where King Bhagiratha is, where Bharata, son of Dushyanta, is: there you will take your pleasure.
